revision.text:
{{Multiple issues| {{Essay-like|date=July 2023}} {{Confusing|date=July 2023|reason=the article is a disorganized jumble of passages about MacArthur}} }} {{Short description|Head of the Allied occupation of Japan}} [[File:GHQ building circa 1950.JPG|thumb|The [[:en:DN Tower 21|Dai-Ichi Seimei Building]] which served as SCAP headquarters, {{circa}} 1950]] The '''Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers''' ({{Langx|ja|連合国軍最高司令官|Rengōkokugun saikōshireikan}}), or '''SCAP''', was the title held by General [[:en:Douglas MacArthur|Douglas MacArthur]] during the [[:en:United States|United States]]-led [[:en:Allies of World War II|Allied]] [[:en:Occupation of Japan|Occupation of Japan]] following [[:en:Pacific War|Pacific War]]. It issued SCAP Directives (alias SCAPIN, SCAP Index Number) to the Japanese government, aiming to suppress its "militaristic nationalism".<ref>{{Cite web| author=S.C.A.P.| date=Jan 4, 1946| url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/9885619?itemId=info%3Andljp%2Fpid%2F9885619&__lang=en| title=Removal and Exclusion of Undesirable Personnel from Public Office| publisher= The National Diet Library (Japan)| access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> The position was created at the start of the occupation of Japan on August 14, 1945.<ref> https://history.army.mil/books/wwii/MacArthur%20Reports/MacArthur%20V1%20Sup/ch3.htm</ref> It was originally styled the '''Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers'''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hellegers |first=Dale M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GL8h6wZPqIoC&pg=PA360 |title=We, the Japanese people |date=2002 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-8032-2 |page=360}}</ref>
In Japan, the position was generally referred to as '''GHQ''' ('''General Headquarters'''), as SCAP also referred to the offices of the occupation (which was officially referred by SCAP itself as {{nihongo|'''General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers'''|連合国軍最高司令官総司令部|Rengōkokugun saikōshireikan sōshireibu|abbreviated as '''GHQ–SCAP'''}}), including a staff of several hundred US [[:en:Civil service|civil servants]] as well as [[:en:military personnel|military personnel]]. Some of these personnel effectively wrote a first draft of the [[:en:Constitution of Japan|Japanese Constitution]], which the [[:en:National Diet|National Diet]] then ratified after a few amendments. [[:en:Australia|Australia]]n, [[:en:United Kingdom|British Empire]], and [[:en:New Zealand|New Zealand]] forces under SCAP were organized into a sub-command known as [[:en:British Commonwealth Occupation Force|British Commonwealth Occupation Force]].
These actions led MacArthur to be viewed as the new Imperial force in Japan by many Japanese political and civilian figures, even being considered to be the rebirth of the ''[[shōgun]]''-style government<ref name="dower">{{cite book |author-link=John W. Dower|last=Dower |first=John W. |date=1999 |title=[[:en:Embracing Defeat|Embracing Defeat: Japan in the Wake of World War II]] |location=New York |publisher=[[:en:W. W. Norton|W. W. Norton]] |isbn=978-0-393-04686-1 |oclc=39143090}}</ref>{{rp|341}} which Japan was ruled under until the start of the [[Meiji Restoration]]. American biographer William Manchester argues that without MacArthur's leadership, Japan would not have been able to make the move from an imperial, totalitarian state, to a democracy. At his appointment, MacArthur announced that he sought to "restore security, dignity and self-respect" to the Japanese people.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Manchester|first1=William|title=American Caesar|date=1978|publisher=Little, Brown and Company|isbn=0-316-54498-1|url=https://archive.org/details/americancaesardo00manc |url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/americancaesardo00manc/page/n503 472]}}</ref>
MacArthur was also in charge of [[:en:United States Army Military Government in Korea|southern Korea]] from 1945 to 1948 due to the lack of clear orders or initiative from Washington, D.C. There was no plan or guideline given to MacArthur from the Joint Chiefs of Staff or the State Department on how to rule Korea, resulting in a tumultuous [[:en:Operation Blacklist Forty|3 year military occupation]] that led to the creation of the U.S.-friendly [[:en:Republic of Korea|Republic of Korea]] in 1948. He ordered Lieutenant General [[:en:John R. Hodge|John R. Hodge]], who accepted the surrender of Japanese forces in southern Korea in September 1945, to govern that area on SCAP's behalf and report to him in Tokyo.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.army.mil/books/wwii/MacArthur%20Reports/MacArthur%20V1%20Sup/ch3.htm |title=CHAPTER III: THE COMMAND STRUCTURE: AFPAC, FEC AND SCAP |website=history.army.mil |access-date=26 March 2021}}{{title missing|date=May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.army.mil/books/pd-c-02.htm |title=CHAPTER II:The House Divided |website=history.army.mil |access-date=26 March 2021}}</ref>
== General MacArthur == {{main |Douglas MacArthur}} [[File:MacArthur_arrives_at_Atsugi;ac01732.jpg|thumb|MacArthur arrives at Atsugi airfield, August 30th, 1945.]] SCAP is oftentimes synonymous with its appointed post war leader, American General Douglas MacArthur. MacArthur ruled Japan with a fairly lenient approach.
As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, MacArthur decided not to prosecute [[Shiro Ishii]] and all members of the [[:en:Unit 731|bacteriological research units]] in exchange for [[:en:germ warfare|germ warfare]] data based on [[:en:human experimentation|human experimentation]]. On May 6, 1947, he wrote to Washington that "additional data, possibly some statements from Ishii probably can be obtained by informing Japanese involved that information will be retained in intelligence channels and will not be employed as 'War Crimes' evidence."<ref>Gold, Hal (2004). ''Unit 731 testimony''. Boston: Tuttle. p. 109. {{ISBN|978-4-900737-39-6}}. {{OCLC|422879915}}.</ref> The deal was concluded in 1948.<ref>Drayton, Richard (May 10, 2005). "An Ethical Blank Cheque: British and US mythology about the second world war ignores our own crimes and legitimises Anglo-American war making". ''[[:en:The Guardian|The Guardian]]''. Archived from the original on January 11, 2012.</ref>
According to historian [[:en:Herbert Bix|Herbert Bix]] in ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]'', "MacArthur's truly extraordinary measures to save the Emperor from trial as a war criminal had a lasting and profoundly distorting impact on Japanese understanding of the lost war."<ref name=":0">[[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix, Herbert P.]] (2000). ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]''. New York: [[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]]. p. 562</ref> MacArthur's reasoning was that if the emperor were executed or sentenced to life imprisonment there would be a violent backlash and revolution from the Japanese of all social classes, and this would interfere with his primary goal of changing Japan from a militarist, feudal society to a pro-Western modern democracy. In a cable sent to General Dwight Eisenhower in February 1946, MacArthur stated that executing or imprisoning the emperor would require the use of one million occupation soldiers to keep the peace.<ref>How the Emperor Became Human (And MacArthur Became Divine)". ''longreads.com''. 11 November 2015. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref>
=== SCAP's relationship with Japanese leadership === [[File:Emperor Hirohito and General MacArthur.jpg|thumb|General MacArthur and Emperor Hirohito, 29th of September, 1945]] The relationship between Japanese leadership and SCAP was tense, as SCAP domineered the former on the path to post war reconstruction. MacArthur was focused on the task at hand, shown by his refusal to address the Japanese leadership or public directly, instead electing to go straight to and from his office every day, without stops. <ref>Watanabe Kenichi Olivier Mille Christine Watanabe ARTE France Kami Productions (Firm) Artline Films and Arte éditions (Firm) dirs. 2009. ''Japan the Emperor and the Army''. Icarus Films.</ref>
MacArthur and SCAP were adamant that the Emperor especially be shielded from responsibility for the war. MacArthur allowed the Emperor to issue statements that allowed for post war SCAP policy to be reframed as continued [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji restoration]], allowing the Emperor to cling to legitimacy. These views would be reflected in the first eight articles of the [[:en:Constitution of Japan|Constitution of Japan]].<ref name=":02">[[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix, Herbert P.]] (2000). ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]''. New York: [[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]]. p. 562</ref>
==Transforming Japan== A major [[:en:Land reform|Land reform]] was conducted, led by [[:en:Wolf Ladejinsky|Wolf Ladejinsky]] of MacArthur's SCAP staff; however, Ladejinsky himself stated that the true architect of the land reform was {{ill|Hiroo Wada|ja|3=和田博雄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hiroo Wada|qq=}}, then-[[:en:Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (Japan)|Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries]] from the [[:en:Japan Socialist Party|Japan Socialist Party]].<ref>{{citation |surname=Ness |given=Gayl D. |year=1967 |title=Review of the book ''Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy: Lord and Peasant in the Making of the Modern World'' |journal=American Sociological Review |volume=32 |issue=5 |pages=818–820 |doi=10.2307/2092029 |jstor=2092029 }}.</ref> Between 1947 and 1949, approximately {{convert|4700000|acre|sigfig=3|abbr=on}}, or 38% of Japan's cultivated land, was purchased from the landlords under the government's reform program, and {{convert|4600000|acre|sigfig=3|abbr=on}} was resold to the farmers who worked them. By 1950, 89% of all agricultural land was owner-operated and only 11% was tenant-operated.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=183–192}} MacArthur's efforts to encourage trade union membership met with phenomenal success, and by 1947, 48% of the non-agricultural workforce was unionized. Some of MacArthur's reforms were rescinded in 1948 when his unilateral control of Japan was ended by the increased involvement of the State Department.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=174–183}} During the Occupation, SCAP successfully, if not entirely, abolished many of the financial coalitions known as the [[:en:Zaibatsu|Zaibatsu]], which had previously monopolized industry.{{sfn|Schaller|1985|p=25}} Eventually, looser industrial groupings known as ''[[:en:Keiretsu|Keiretsu]]'' evolved. The reforms alarmed many in the U.S. Departments of Defense and State, who believed they conflicted with the prospect of Japan and its industrial capacity as a bulwark against the spread of communism in Asia.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=222–224, 252–254}}
Japan's hereditary peerage, called [[kazoku]], that lasted for over a millennium in different but essentially similar forms, was abolished by the new Japanese constitution that was heavily influenced by MacArthur. This was similar to the European peerage system involving princes, barons and counts that were not part of the royal family. Also, the extended royal family, called [[:en:Ōke|Ōke]] and [[shinnōke]], was abolished and stripped of all rights and privileges, transforming into commoners immediately. The only Japanese that were allowed to call themselves a part of royalty or nobility after the U.S. occupation were the emperor and about 20 of his [[Imperial House of Japan#List of current members|direct family members]]. This action by MacArthur and the writers of the constitution helped transform Japan drastically by abolishing all of the old extended royal family class and the nobility class.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/macarthur-occupation-japan-and-constitution/ |title=Occupation of Japan and the New Constitution | American Experience | PBS |website=www.pbs.org |access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>
==Welfare programs== One of the largest of the SCAP programs was Public Health and Welfare, headed by US Army Colonel Crawford F. Sams. Working with the SCAP staff of 150, Sams directed the welfare work of the American doctors, and organized entirely new Japanese medical welfare systems along American lines. The Japanese population was in a poor state: most people were badly worn down, doctors and medicines were very scarce, and sanitary systems had been bombed out in larger cities. Sams' earliest priorities were in distributing food supplies from the United States. Millions of refugees from the defunct overseas empire were pouring in, often in bad physical shape, with a high risk of introducing [[:en:Smallpox|Smallpox]], [[typhus]] and [[:en:Cholera|Cholera]]. The outbreaks that did occur were localized, as emergency immunization, quarantine, sanitation, and delousing prevented massive epidemics. Sams, who was promoted to Brigadier General in 1948, worked with Japanese officials to establish vaccine laboratories, reorganize hospitals along American lines, upgrade medical and nursing schools, and bring together Japanese, international, and US teams that dealt with disasters, child care, and health insurance. He set up an Institute of Public Health for educating public health workers and a National Institute of Health for research, and set up statistical divisions and data collection systems.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Crawford F. |last=Sams |title="Medic": The Mission of an American Military Doctor in Occupied Japan and Wartorn Korea |date=1998 |isbn=978-1-315-50371-4 |publisher=Routledge}}</ref>
== Constitution == {{Main |Constitution of Japan}}
One of the most significant actions of SCAP during the occupation was the drafting of a new Japanese constitution. One of MacArthur's top priorities was an overhaul of the existing [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]], to bring the country in line with its new democratic government. He gave the task of drafting the constitution to his officers, frustrated by the slowness of legislators. They would finish the task within a week, and presenting the new constitution as a wholesale amendment to the [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]]. It provided protections to the Emperor, placing him at the head of the state. It was ratified November of 1946 and went into effect May 3rd, 1947. It remains the oldest unamended constitution in the world. <ref>"The Anomalous Life of the Japanese Constitution". ''Nippon.com''. 15 August 2017. Archived from the original on 11 August 2019.</ref>
=== Article 9 === The most polarizing aspect of the Japanese constitution, a part that still sees debate to this day, is the presence of [[:en:Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution|Article 9]], a clause covering the status of the Japanese military. The clause outlaws belligerency and prohibits the establishment of organized armed forces by the government. Despite this, Japan maintains a "[[:en:Japan Self-Defense Forces|self defense force]]" (a de facto defensive military) of around 250,000 active personnel. Article 9 and the [[:en:Japan Self-Defense Forces|JSDF]] are both hotly contested subjects of debates in modern Japanese politics, as pacifists see the JSDF and [[:en:Military history of Japan|military involvement]] in foreign countries as unconstitutional, while nationalists seek [[:en:Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution|Article 9]]'s removal and a wider rearmament of Japan.
==War crimes issues== SCAP arrested 28 suspected war criminals on account of crimes against peace, but it did not conduct the Tokyo Trials; the [[:en:International Military Tribunal for the Far East|International Military Tribunal for the Far East]] was responsible instead.<ref>{{cite book |first=Timothy P. |last=Maga |title=Judgment at Tokyo: The Japanese War Crimes Trials |date=2001 |publisher=University Press of Kentucky |isbn=978-0-8131-2177-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first=Yuki |last=Tanaka |display-authors=etal |title=Beyond Victor's Justice? The Tokyo War Crimes Trial Revisited|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nOIzDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA149|year=2011|publisher=BRILL|pages=149–50 |isbn=978-90-04-21591-7}}</ref> [[:en:President of the United States|President]] [[:en:Harry S. Truman|Harry Truman]] had negotiated Japanese surrender on the condition the Emperor would not be executed or put on trial. SCAP carried out that policy.<ref>{{cite book|first=Paul |last=Ham|title=Hiroshima Nagasaki: The Real Story of the Atomic Bombings and Their Aftermath|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5FZGAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA79|year=2014|publisher=St. Martin's Press|pages=79–80 |isbn=978-1-4668-4747-7}}</ref>
As soon as November 26, 1945, MacArthur confirmed to Admiral [[:en:Mitsumasa Yonai|Mitsumasa Yonai]] that the emperor's abdication would not be necessary.{{r|dower|page1=323}} Before the war crimes trials actually convened, SCAP, the IPS and officials from [[:en:Hirohito|Hirohito]]'s [[Shōwa period|Shōwa]] government worked behind the scenes not only to prevent the imperial family being indicted, but also to slant the testimony of the defendants to ensure that no one implicated the Emperor. High officials in court circles and the Shōwa government collaborated with Allied GHQ in compiling lists of prospective [[:en:war criminals|war criminals]], while the individuals arrested as ''Class A'' suspects and incarcerated in [[:en:Sugamo Prison|Sugamo Prison]] solemnly vowed to protect their sovereign against any possible taint of war responsibility.{{r|dower|page1=325}}
As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, MacArthur also decided not to prosecute [[Shiro Ishii]] and all members of the [[:en:Unit 731|bacteriological research units]] in exchange for [[:en:germ warfare|germ warfare]] data based on [[:en:human experimentation|human experimentation]]. On May 6, 1947, he wrote to Washington that "additional data, possibly some statements from Ishii probably can be obtained by informing Japanese involved that information will be retained in intelligence channels and will not be employed as "War Crimes" evidence."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gold |first1=Hal |title=Unit 731 testimony |date=2004 |publisher=Tuttle |location=Boston |isbn=978-4-900737-39-6 |oclc=422879915 |page=[https://archive.org/details/unit731testimony00halg/page/109 109] |url=https://archive.org/details/unit731testimony00halg/page/109 }}</ref> The deal was concluded in 1948.<ref>{{cite news |last=Drayton |first=Richard |date=May 10, 2005 |url=http://www.commondreams.org/views05/0510-24.htm |title=An Ethical Blank Cheque: British and US mythology about the second world war ignores our own crimes and legitimises Anglo-American war making |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111112521/http://www.commondreams.org/views05/0510-24.htm |archive-date=January 11, 2012 |work=[[:en:The Guardian|The Guardian]]}}</ref>
According to historian [[:en:Herbert Bix|Herbert Bix]] in ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]'', "MacArthur's truly extraordinary measures to save the Emperor from trial as a war criminal had a lasting and profoundly distorting impact on Japanese understanding of the lost war."<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Herbert Bix |last=Bix |first=Herbert P. |date=2000 |title=[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]] |location=New York |publisher=[[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]] |isbn=978-0-06-019314-0 |oclc=247018161 |page=545}}</ref> MacArthur's reasoning was if the emperor were executed or sentenced to life imprisonment there would be a violent backlash and revolution from the Japanese from all social classes and this would interfere with his primary goal to change Japan from a militarist, feudal society to a pro-Western modern democracy. In a cable sent to General Dwight Eisenhower in February 1946 MacArthur said executing or imprisoning the emperor would require the use of one million occupation soldiers to keep the peace.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://longreads.com/2015/11/11/how-the-emperor-became-human-and-macarthur-became-divine/ |title=How the Emperor Became Human (And MacArthur Became Divine) |website=longreads.com |date= 11 November 2015|access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>
==Media censorship== Above the political and economic control SCAP had for the seven years following Japan's surrender, SCAP also had strict control over all of the Japanese media, under the formation of the [[:en:Civil Censorship Detachment|Civil Censorship Detachment]] (CCD) of SCAP. The CCD eventually banned a total of 31 topics from all forms of media.{{r|dower|page1=341}} These topics included:
* Criticism of SCAP (individuals and the organization). * All Allied countries. * Criticism of Allied policy pre- and post-war. * Any form of [[:en:Empire of Japan|imperial]] propaganda. * Defense of [[:en:Japanese war crimes|war criminals]]. * Praise of "undemocratic" [[:en:Form of government|forms of government]], though praise of SCAP itself was permitted. * The [[:en:Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]]. * [[:en:Underground economy|Black market]] activities. * Open discussion of allied diplomatic relations ([[Soviet Union–United States relations]]).
Although some of the CCD censorship laws considerably relaxed towards the end of SCAP, some topics, like the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, were taboo until 1952 at the end of the occupation.
== Approach to the Japanese Communist Party and Post-War Reforms ==
{{Essay-like|section|date=July 2023}}
MacArthur legalized the [[:en:Japanese Communist Party|Japanese Communist Party]] despite reservations from the United States government and invited them to take part in the [[:en:1946 Japanese general election|1946 election]], which was also the first ever Japanese election to allow women to vote. He ordered the release of all political prisoners of the Imperial Japanese era, including communist prisoners. MacArthur approved the first May Day parade in 11 years in 1946. On the day before the May Day celebrations, which would involve 300,000 Japanese communists demonstrating with red flags and pro-Marxism chants in front of the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]] and the [[:en:DN Tower 21|Dai-Ichi Building]], a group of would-be assassins led by Hideo Tokayama that planned to assassinate MacArthur with hand grenades and pistols on May Day was stopped and some of its members arrested. Despite this plot the May Day demonstrations went on. MacArthur stopped the Communist Party from gaining any popularity in Japan by releasing their members from prison, conducting landmark land reform for the rural Japanese farmers and peasants, and allowing the communists to freely participate in elections. In the 1946 election they won only 6 seats.<ref>Morris Jr., Seymour. ''Supreme Commander: MacArthur's Triumph in Japan''. Page 169-173</ref><ref>"MacArthur Plot Alarms Japanese; They See Possible Repercussions; JAPANESE FEARFUL ON M'ARTHUR PLOT Timed for Demonstration Plotters Still at Large". ''The New York Times''. May 1946. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref><ref>"Gettysburg Times - Google News Archive Search". ''news.google.com''. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref>
== Legacy ==
[[File:Yoshida_signs_San_Francisco_Peace_Treaty.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Shigeru Yoshida|Shigeru Yoshida]], [[:en:Prime Minister of Japan|Prime Minister of Japan]] signing the San Francisco Peace Treaty on September 8, 1951]] MacArthur handed over power to the Japanese government in 1949, but remained in Japan until relieved by President [[:en:Harry S. Truman|Harry S. Truman]] on 11 April 1951, after which he was succeeded as SCAP by General [[:en:Matthew Ridgway|Matthew Ridgway]]. The [[:en:San Francisco Peace Treaty|San Francisco Peace Treaty]], signed on 8 September 1951, marked the end of the Allied occupation, and when it went into effect on 28 April 1952, Japan was once again an independent state. The position of SCAP was effectively abolished on 1 July 1957 with the disbandment of the [[:en:Far East Command (United States)|Far East Command]]. However, the United States continued to administer some Japanese islands after that with, for example, Okinawa being continually under US administration until 1972.<ref>USFJ (May 13, 2022). "United States Forces Japan". US Forces Japan. Retrieved 2019-02-20.</ref>
=== Active US military presence === {{Main |United States Forces Japan}} All branches of the United States military forces are still present in Japan today. They primarily function in a support role, providing defense for Japan and the surrounding region, per the agreements of the [[Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan|US-Japan Mutual Security Treaty.]] The [[:en:United States Forces Japan|United States Forces Japan]] consists of around 50,000 service members deployed all over Japan to protect Japanese and US interests alike. This has led to tension at times between Japanese citizens and American servicemen, with incidents frequently occurring between locals and servicemen and crimes frequently committed by servicemen against locals, such as the [[:en:1995 Okinawa rape incident|1995 Okinawa rape incident]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spitzer |first=Kirk |title=Tens of thousands protest on Okinawa to close key U.S. bases in Japan |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2016/06/19/okinawa-protest-marines/86110434/ |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2024-06-28 |title=Second U.S. service member in months charged with rape in Japan's Okinawa: "We are outraged" - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/second-us-soldier-japan-charged-sexual-assault-okinawa/ |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref> These incidents led to plans to relocate military bases in [[:en:Okinawa Prefecture|Okinawa]], namely [[:en:Marine Corps Air Station Futenma|Marine Corps Air Station Futenma]], as three quarters of all USFJ installations are located in the prefecture, despite its small size. However, the plan has been delayed due to protests at the site designated for its relocation on another part of the island.<ref name=":1" />

{{Multiple issues| {{Essay-like|date=July 2023}} {{Confusing|date=July 2023|reason=the article is a disorganized jumble of passages about MacArthur}} }} {{Short description|Head of the Allied occupation of Japan}} [[File:GHQ building circa 1950.JPG|thumb|The [[:en:DN Tower 21|Dai-Ichi Seimei Building]] which served as SCAP headquarters, {{circa}} 1950]] The '''Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers''' ({{Langx|ja|連合国軍最高司令官|Rengōkokugun saikōshireikan}}), or '''SCAP''', was the title held by General [[:en:Douglas MacArthur|Douglas MacArthur]] during the [[:en:United States|United States]]-led [[:en:Allies of World War II|Allied]] [[:en:Occupation of Japan|Occupation of Japan]] following [[:en:Pacific War|Pacific War]]. It issued SCAP Directives (alias SCAPIN, SCAP Index Number) to the Japanese government, aiming to suppress its "militaristic nationalism".<ref>{{Cite web| author=S.C.A.P.| date=Jan 4, 1946| url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/9885619?itemId=info%3Andljp%2Fpid%2F9885619&__lang=en| title=Removal and Exclusion of Undesirable Personnel from Public Office| publisher= The National Diet Library (Japan)| access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> The position was created at the start of the occupation of Japan on August 14, 1945.<ref> https://history.army.mil/books/wwii/MacArthur%20Reports/MacArthur%20V1%20Sup/ch3.htm</ref> It was originally styled the '''Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers'''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hellegers |first=Dale M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GL8h6wZPqIoC&pg=PA360 |title=We, the Japanese people |date=2002 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-8032-2 |page=360}}</ref>
In Japan, the position was generally referred to as '''GHQ''' ('''General Headquarters'''), as SCAP also referred to the offices of the occupation (which was officially referred by SCAP itself as {{nihongo|'''General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers'''|連合国軍最高司令官総司令部|Rengōkokugun saikōshireikan sōshireibu|abbreviated as '''GHQ–SCAP'''}}), including a staff of several hundred US [[:en:Civil service|civil servants]] as well as [[:en:military personnel|military personnel]]. Some of these personnel effectively wrote a first draft of the [[:en:Constitution of Japan|Japanese Constitution]], which the [[:en:National Diet|National Diet]] then ratified after a few amendments. [[:en:Australia|Australia]]n, [[:en:United Kingdom|British Empire]], and [[:en:New Zealand|New Zealand]] forces under SCAP were organized into a sub-command known as [[:en:British Commonwealth Occupation Force|British Commonwealth Occupation Force]].
These actions led MacArthur to be viewed as the new Imperial force in Japan by many Japanese political and civilian figures, even being considered to be the rebirth of the ''[[shōgun]]''-style government<ref name="dower">{{cite book |author-link=John W. Dower|last=Dower |first=John W. |date=1999 |title=[[:en:Embracing Defeat|Embracing Defeat: Japan in the Wake of World War II]] |location=New York |publisher=[[:en:W. W. Norton|W. W. Norton]] |isbn=978-0-393-04686-1 |oclc=39143090}}</ref>{{rp|341}} which Japan was ruled under until the start of the [[Meiji Restoration]]. American biographer William Manchester argues that without MacArthur's leadership, Japan would not have been able to make the move from an imperial, totalitarian state, to a democracy. At his appointment, MacArthur announced that he sought to "restore security, dignity and self-respect" to the Japanese people.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Manchester|first1=William|title=American Caesar|date=1978|publisher=Little, Brown and Company|isbn=0-316-54498-1|url=https://archive.org/details/americancaesardo00manc |url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/americancaesardo00manc/page/n503 472]}}</ref>
MacArthur was also in charge of [[:en:United States Army Military Government in Korea|southern Korea]] from 1945 to 1948 due to the lack of clear orders or initiative from Washington, D.C. There was no plan or guideline given to MacArthur from the Joint Chiefs of Staff or the State Department on how to rule Korea, resulting in a tumultuous [[:en:Operation Blacklist Forty|3 year military occupation]] that led to the creation of the U.S.-friendly [[:en:Republic of Korea|Republic of Korea]] in 1948. He ordered Lieutenant General [[:en:John R. Hodge|John R. Hodge]], who accepted the surrender of Japanese forces in southern Korea in September 1945, to govern that area on SCAP's behalf and report to him in Tokyo.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.army.mil/books/wwii/MacArthur%20Reports/MacArthur%20V1%20Sup/ch3.htm |title=CHAPTER III: THE COMMAND STRUCTURE: AFPAC, FEC AND SCAP |website=history.army.mil |access-date=26 March 2021}}{{title missing|date=May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.army.mil/books/pd-c-02.htm |title=CHAPTER II:The House Divided |website=history.army.mil |access-date=26 March 2021}}</ref>
== General MacArthur == {{main |Douglas MacArthur}} [[File:MacArthur_arrives_at_Atsugi;ac01732.jpg|thumb|MacArthur arrives at Atsugi airfield, August 30th, 1945.]] SCAP is oftentimes synonymous with its appointed post war leader, American General Douglas MacArthur. MacArthur ruled Japan with a fairly lenient approach.
As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, MacArthur decided not to prosecute [[Shiro Ishii]] and all members of the [[:en:Unit 731|bacteriological research units]] in exchange for [[:en:germ warfare|germ warfare]] data based on [[:en:human experimentation|human experimentation]]. On May 6, 1947, he wrote to Washington that "additional data, possibly some statements from Ishii probably can be obtained by informing Japanese involved that information will be retained in intelligence channels and will not be employed as 'War Crimes' evidence."<ref>Gold, Hal (2004). ''Unit 731 testimony''. Boston: Tuttle. p. 109. {{ISBN|978-4-900737-39-6}}. {{OCLC|422879915}}.</ref> The deal was concluded in 1948.<ref>Drayton, Richard (May 10, 2005). "An Ethical Blank Cheque: British and US mythology about the second world war ignores our own crimes and legitimises Anglo-American war making". ''[[:en:The Guardian|The Guardian]]''. Archived from the original on January 11, 2012.</ref>
According to historian [[:en:Herbert Bix|Herbert Bix]] in ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]'', "MacArthur's truly extraordinary measures to save the Emperor from trial as a war criminal had a lasting and profoundly distorting impact on Japanese understanding of the lost war."<ref name=":0">[[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix, Herbert P.]] (2000). ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]''. New York: [[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]]. p. 562</ref> MacArthur's reasoning was that if the emperor were executed or sentenced to life imprisonment there would be a violent backlash and revolution from the Japanese of all social classes, and this would interfere with his primary goal of changing Japan from a militarist, feudal society to a pro-Western modern democracy. In a cable sent to General Dwight Eisenhower in February 1946, MacArthur stated that executing or imprisoning the emperor would require the use of one million occupation soldiers to keep the peace.<ref>How the Emperor Became Human (And MacArthur Became Divine)". ''longreads.com''. 11 November 2015. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref>
=== SCAP's relationship with Japanese leadership === [[File:Emperor Hirohito and General MacArthur.jpg|thumb|General MacArthur and Emperor Hirohito, 29th of September, 1945]] The relationship between Japanese leadership and SCAP was tense, as SCAP domineered the former on the path to post war reconstruction. MacArthur was focused on the task at hand, shown by his refusal to address the Japanese leadership or public directly, instead electing to go straight to and from his office every day, without stops. <ref>Watanabe Kenichi Olivier Mille Christine Watanabe ARTE France Kami Productions (Firm) Artline Films and Arte éditions (Firm) dirs. 2009. ''Japan the Emperor and the Army''. Icarus Films.</ref>
MacArthur and SCAP were adamant that the Emperor especially be shielded from responsibility for the war. MacArthur allowed the Emperor to issue statements that allowed for post war SCAP policy to be reframed as continued [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji restoration]], allowing the Emperor to cling to legitimacy. These views would be reflected in the first eight articles of the [[:en:Constitution of Japan|Constitution of Japan]].<ref name=":02">[[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix, Herbert P.]] (2000). ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]''. New York: [[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]]. p. 562</ref>
==Transforming Japan== A major [[:en:Land reform|Land reform]] was conducted, led by [[:en:Wolf Ladejinsky|Wolf Ladejinsky]] of MacArthur's SCAP staff; however, Ladejinsky himself stated that the true architect of the land reform was {{ill|Hiroo Wada|ja|3=和田博雄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hiroo Wada|qq=}}, then-[[:en:Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (Japan)|Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries]] from the [[:en:Japan Socialist Party|Japan Socialist Party]].<ref>{{citation |surname=Ness |given=Gayl D. |year=1967 |title=Review of the book ''Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy: Lord and Peasant in the Making of the Modern World'' |journal=American Sociological Review |volume=32 |issue=5 |pages=818–820 |doi=10.2307/2092029 |jstor=2092029 }}.</ref> Between 1947 and 1949, approximately {{convert|4700000|acre|sigfig=3|abbr=on}}, or 38% of Japan's cultivated land, was purchased from the landlords under the government's reform program, and {{convert|4600000|acre|sigfig=3|abbr=on}} was resold to the farmers who worked them. By 1950, 89% of all agricultural land was owner-operated and only 11% was tenant-operated.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=183–192}} MacArthur's efforts to encourage trade union membership met with phenomenal success, and by 1947, 48% of the non-agricultural workforce was unionized. Some of MacArthur's reforms were rescinded in 1948 when his unilateral control of Japan was ended by the increased involvement of the State Department.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=174–183}} During the Occupation, SCAP successfully, if not entirely, abolished many of the financial coalitions known as the [[:en:Zaibatsu|Zaibatsu]], which had previously monopolized industry.{{sfn|Schaller|1985|p=25}} Eventually, looser industrial groupings known as ''[[:en:Keiretsu|Keiretsu]]'' evolved. The reforms alarmed many in the U.S. Departments of Defense and State, who believed they conflicted with the prospect of Japan and its industrial capacity as a bulwark against the spread of communism in Asia.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=222–224, 252–254}}
Japan's hereditary peerage, called [[kazoku]], that lasted for over a millennium in different but essentially similar forms, was abolished by the new Japanese constitution that was heavily influenced by MacArthur. This was similar to the European peerage system involving princes, barons and counts that were not part of the royal family. Also, the extended royal family, called [[:en:Ōke|Ōke]] and [[:en:Shinnōke|Shinnōke]], was abolished and stripped of all rights and privileges, transforming into commoners immediately. The only Japanese that were allowed to call themselves a part of royalty or nobility after the U.S. occupation were the emperor and about 20 of his [[Imperial House of Japan#List of current members|direct family members]]. This action by MacArthur and the writers of the constitution helped transform Japan drastically by abolishing all of the old extended royal family class and the nobility class.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/macarthur-occupation-japan-and-constitution/ |title=Occupation of Japan and the New Constitution | American Experience | PBS |website=www.pbs.org |access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>
==Welfare programs== One of the largest of the SCAP programs was Public Health and Welfare, headed by US Army Colonel Crawford F. Sams. Working with the SCAP staff of 150, Sams directed the welfare work of the American doctors, and organized entirely new Japanese medical welfare systems along American lines. The Japanese population was in a poor state: most people were badly worn down, doctors and medicines were very scarce, and sanitary systems had been bombed out in larger cities. Sams' earliest priorities were in distributing food supplies from the United States. Millions of refugees from the defunct overseas empire were pouring in, often in bad physical shape, with a high risk of introducing [[:en:Smallpox|Smallpox]], [[typhus]] and [[:en:Cholera|Cholera]]. The outbreaks that did occur were localized, as emergency immunization, quarantine, sanitation, and delousing prevented massive epidemics. Sams, who was promoted to Brigadier General in 1948, worked with Japanese officials to establish vaccine laboratories, reorganize hospitals along American lines, upgrade medical and nursing schools, and bring together Japanese, international, and US teams that dealt with disasters, child care, and health insurance. He set up an Institute of Public Health for educating public health workers and a National Institute of Health for research, and set up statistical divisions and data collection systems.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Crawford F. |last=Sams |title="Medic": The Mission of an American Military Doctor in Occupied Japan and Wartorn Korea |date=1998 |isbn=978-1-315-50371-4 |publisher=Routledge}}</ref>
== Constitution == {{Main |Constitution of Japan}}
One of the most significant actions of SCAP during the occupation was the drafting of a new Japanese constitution. One of MacArthur's top priorities was an overhaul of the existing [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]], to bring the country in line with its new democratic government. He gave the task of drafting the constitution to his officers, frustrated by the slowness of legislators. They would finish the task within a week, and presenting the new constitution as a wholesale amendment to the [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]]. It provided protections to the Emperor, placing him at the head of the state. It was ratified November of 1946 and went into effect May 3rd, 1947. It remains the oldest unamended constitution in the world. <ref>"The Anomalous Life of the Japanese Constitution". ''Nippon.com''. 15 August 2017. Archived from the original on 11 August 2019.</ref>
=== Article 9 === The most polarizing aspect of the Japanese constitution, a part that still sees debate to this day, is the presence of [[:en:Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution|Article 9]], a clause covering the status of the Japanese military. The clause outlaws belligerency and prohibits the establishment of organized armed forces by the government. Despite this, Japan maintains a "[[:en:Japan Self-Defense Forces|self defense force]]" (a de facto defensive military) of around 250,000 active personnel. Article 9 and the [[:en:Japan Self-Defense Forces|JSDF]] are both hotly contested subjects of debates in modern Japanese politics, as pacifists see the JSDF and [[:en:Military history of Japan|military involvement]] in foreign countries as unconstitutional, while nationalists seek [[:en:Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution|Article 9]]'s removal and a wider rearmament of Japan.
==War crimes issues== SCAP arrested 28 suspected war criminals on account of crimes against peace, but it did not conduct the Tokyo Trials; the [[:en:International Military Tribunal for the Far East|International Military Tribunal for the Far East]] was responsible instead.<ref>{{cite book |first=Timothy P. |last=Maga |title=Judgment at Tokyo: The Japanese War Crimes Trials |date=2001 |publisher=University Press of Kentucky |isbn=978-0-8131-2177-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first=Yuki |last=Tanaka |display-authors=etal |title=Beyond Victor's Justice? The Tokyo War Crimes Trial Revisited|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nOIzDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA149|year=2011|publisher=BRILL|pages=149–50 |isbn=978-90-04-21591-7}}</ref> [[:en:President of the United States|President]] [[:en:Harry S. Truman|Harry Truman]] had negotiated Japanese surrender on the condition the Emperor would not be executed or put on trial. SCAP carried out that policy.<ref>{{cite book|first=Paul |last=Ham|title=Hiroshima Nagasaki: The Real Story of the Atomic Bombings and Their Aftermath|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5FZGAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA79|year=2014|publisher=St. Martin's Press|pages=79–80 |isbn=978-1-4668-4747-7}}</ref>
As soon as November 26, 1945, MacArthur confirmed to Admiral [[:en:Mitsumasa Yonai|Mitsumasa Yonai]] that the emperor's abdication would not be necessary.{{r|dower|page1=323}} Before the war crimes trials actually convened, SCAP, the IPS and officials from [[:en:Hirohito|Hirohito]]'s [[Shōwa period|Shōwa]] government worked behind the scenes not only to prevent the imperial family being indicted, but also to slant the testimony of the defendants to ensure that no one implicated the Emperor. High officials in court circles and the Shōwa government collaborated with Allied GHQ in compiling lists of prospective [[:en:war criminals|war criminals]], while the individuals arrested as ''Class A'' suspects and incarcerated in [[:en:Sugamo Prison|Sugamo Prison]] solemnly vowed to protect their sovereign against any possible taint of war responsibility.{{r|dower|page1=325}}
As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, MacArthur also decided not to prosecute [[Shiro Ishii]] and all members of the [[:en:Unit 731|bacteriological research units]] in exchange for [[:en:germ warfare|germ warfare]] data based on [[:en:human experimentation|human experimentation]]. On May 6, 1947, he wrote to Washington that "additional data, possibly some statements from Ishii probably can be obtained by informing Japanese involved that information will be retained in intelligence channels and will not be employed as "War Crimes" evidence."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gold |first1=Hal |title=Unit 731 testimony |date=2004 |publisher=Tuttle |location=Boston |isbn=978-4-900737-39-6 |oclc=422879915 |page=[https://archive.org/details/unit731testimony00halg/page/109 109] |url=https://archive.org/details/unit731testimony00halg/page/109 }}</ref> The deal was concluded in 1948.<ref>{{cite news |last=Drayton |first=Richard |date=May 10, 2005 |url=http://www.commondreams.org/views05/0510-24.htm |title=An Ethical Blank Cheque: British and US mythology about the second world war ignores our own crimes and legitimises Anglo-American war making |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111112521/http://www.commondreams.org/views05/0510-24.htm |archive-date=January 11, 2012 |work=[[:en:The Guardian|The Guardian]]}}</ref>
According to historian [[:en:Herbert Bix|Herbert Bix]] in ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]'', "MacArthur's truly extraordinary measures to save the Emperor from trial as a war criminal had a lasting and profoundly distorting impact on Japanese understanding of the lost war."<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Herbert Bix |last=Bix |first=Herbert P. |date=2000 |title=[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]] |location=New York |publisher=[[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]] |isbn=978-0-06-019314-0 |oclc=247018161 |page=545}}</ref> MacArthur's reasoning was if the emperor were executed or sentenced to life imprisonment there would be a violent backlash and revolution from the Japanese from all social classes and this would interfere with his primary goal to change Japan from a militarist, feudal society to a pro-Western modern democracy. In a cable sent to General Dwight Eisenhower in February 1946 MacArthur said executing or imprisoning the emperor would require the use of one million occupation soldiers to keep the peace.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://longreads.com/2015/11/11/how-the-emperor-became-human-and-macarthur-became-divine/ |title=How the Emperor Became Human (And MacArthur Became Divine) |website=longreads.com |date= 11 November 2015|access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>
==Media censorship== Above the political and economic control SCAP had for the seven years following Japan's surrender, SCAP also had strict control over all of the Japanese media, under the formation of the [[:en:Civil Censorship Detachment|Civil Censorship Detachment]] (CCD) of SCAP. The CCD eventually banned a total of 31 topics from all forms of media.{{r|dower|page1=341}} These topics included:
* Criticism of SCAP (individuals and the organization). * All Allied countries. * Criticism of Allied policy pre- and post-war. * Any form of [[:en:Empire of Japan|imperial]] propaganda. * Defense of [[:en:Japanese war crimes|war criminals]]. * Praise of "undemocratic" [[:en:Form of government|forms of government]], though praise of SCAP itself was permitted. * The [[:en:Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]]. * [[:en:Underground economy|Black market]] activities. * Open discussion of allied diplomatic relations ([[Soviet Union–United States relations]]).
Although some of the CCD censorship laws considerably relaxed towards the end of SCAP, some topics, like the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, were taboo until 1952 at the end of the occupation.
== Approach to the Japanese Communist Party and Post-War Reforms ==
{{Essay-like|section|date=July 2023}}
MacArthur legalized the [[:en:Japanese Communist Party|Japanese Communist Party]] despite reservations from the United States government and invited them to take part in the [[:en:1946 Japanese general election|1946 election]], which was also the first ever Japanese election to allow women to vote. He ordered the release of all political prisoners of the Imperial Japanese era, including communist prisoners. MacArthur approved the first May Day parade in 11 years in 1946. On the day before the May Day celebrations, which would involve 300,000 Japanese communists demonstrating with red flags and pro-Marxism chants in front of the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]] and the [[:en:DN Tower 21|Dai-Ichi Building]], a group of would-be assassins led by Hideo Tokayama that planned to assassinate MacArthur with hand grenades and pistols on May Day was stopped and some of its members arrested. Despite this plot the May Day demonstrations went on. MacArthur stopped the Communist Party from gaining any popularity in Japan by releasing their members from prison, conducting landmark land reform for the rural Japanese farmers and peasants, and allowing the communists to freely participate in elections. In the 1946 election they won only 6 seats.<ref>Morris Jr., Seymour. ''Supreme Commander: MacArthur's Triumph in Japan''. Page 169-173</ref><ref>"MacArthur Plot Alarms Japanese; They See Possible Repercussions; JAPANESE FEARFUL ON M'ARTHUR PLOT Timed for Demonstration Plotters Still at Large". ''The New York Times''. May 1946. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref><ref>"Gettysburg Times - Google News Archive Search". ''news.google.com''. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref>
== Legacy ==
[[File:Yoshida_signs_San_Francisco_Peace_Treaty.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Shigeru Yoshida|Shigeru Yoshida]], [[:en:Prime Minister of Japan|Prime Minister of Japan]] signing the San Francisco Peace Treaty on September 8, 1951]] MacArthur handed over power to the Japanese government in 1949, but remained in Japan until relieved by President [[:en:Harry S. Truman|Harry S. Truman]] on 11 April 1951, after which he was succeeded as SCAP by General [[:en:Matthew Ridgway|Matthew Ridgway]]. The [[:en:San Francisco Peace Treaty|San Francisco Peace Treaty]], signed on 8 September 1951, marked the end of the Allied occupation, and when it went into effect on 28 April 1952, Japan was once again an independent state. The position of SCAP was effectively abolished on 1 July 1957 with the disbandment of the [[:en:Far East Command (United States)|Far East Command]]. However, the United States continued to administer some Japanese islands after that with, for example, Okinawa being continually under US administration until 1972.<ref>USFJ (May 13, 2022). "United States Forces Japan". US Forces Japan. Retrieved 2019-02-20.</ref>
=== Active US military presence === {{Main |United States Forces Japan}} All branches of the United States military forces are still present in Japan today. They primarily function in a support role, providing defense for Japan and the surrounding region, per the agreements of the [[Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan|US-Japan Mutual Security Treaty.]] The [[:en:United States Forces Japan|United States Forces Japan]] consists of around 50,000 service members deployed all over Japan to protect Japanese and US interests alike. This has led to tension at times between Japanese citizens and American servicemen, with incidents frequently occurring between locals and servicemen and crimes frequently committed by servicemen against locals, such as the [[:en:1995 Okinawa rape incident|1995 Okinawa rape incident]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spitzer |first=Kirk |title=Tens of thousands protest on Okinawa to close key U.S. bases in Japan |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2016/06/19/okinawa-protest-marines/86110434/ |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2024-06-28 |title=Second U.S. service member in months charged with rape in Japan's Okinawa: "We are outraged" - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/second-us-soldier-japan-charged-sexual-assault-okinawa/ |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref> These incidents led to plans to relocate military bases in [[:en:Okinawa Prefecture|Okinawa]], namely [[:en:Marine Corps Air Station Futenma|Marine Corps Air Station Futenma]], as three quarters of all USFJ installations are located in the prefecture, despite its small size. However, the plan has been delayed due to protests at the site designated for its relocation on another part of the island.<ref name=":1" />

revision.text:
{{Multiple issues| {{Essay-like|date=July 2023}} {{Confusing|date=July 2023|reason=the article is a disorganized jumble of passages about MacArthur}} }} {{Short description|Head of the Allied occupation of Japan}} [[File:GHQ building circa 1950.JPG|thumb|The [[:en:DN Tower 21|Dai-Ichi Seimei Building]] which served as SCAP headquarters, {{circa}} 1950]] The '''Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers''' ({{Langx|ja|連合国軍最高司令官|Rengōkokugun saikōshireikan}}), or '''SCAP''', was the title held by General [[:en:Douglas MacArthur|Douglas MacArthur]] during the [[:en:United States|United States]]-led [[:en:Allies of World War II|Allied]] [[:en:Occupation of Japan|Occupation of Japan]] following [[:en:Pacific War|Pacific War]]. It issued SCAP Directives (alias SCAPIN, SCAP Index Number) to the Japanese government, aiming to suppress its "militaristic nationalism".<ref>{{Cite web| author=S.C.A.P.| date=Jan 4, 1946| url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/9885619?itemId=info%3Andljp%2Fpid%2F9885619&__lang=en| title=Removal and Exclusion of Undesirable Personnel from Public Office| publisher= The National Diet Library (Japan)| access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> The position was created at the start of the occupation of Japan on August 14, 1945.<ref> https://history.army.mil/books/wwii/MacArthur%20Reports/MacArthur%20V1%20Sup/ch3.htm</ref> It was originally styled the '''Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers'''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hellegers |first=Dale M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GL8h6wZPqIoC&pg=PA360 |title=We, the Japanese people |date=2002 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-8032-2 |page=360}}</ref>
In Japan, the position was generally referred to as '''GHQ''' ('''General Headquarters'''), as SCAP also referred to the offices of the occupation (which was officially referred by SCAP itself as {{nihongo|'''General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers'''|連合国軍最高司令官総司令部|Rengōkokugun saikōshireikan sōshireibu|abbreviated as '''GHQ–SCAP'''}}), including a staff of several hundred US [[:en:Civil service|civil servants]] as well as [[:en:military personnel|military personnel]]. Some of these personnel effectively wrote a first draft of the [[:en:Constitution of Japan|Japanese Constitution]], which the [[:en:National Diet|National Diet]] then ratified after a few amendments. [[:en:Australia|Australia]]n, [[:en:United Kingdom|British Empire]], and [[:en:New Zealand|New Zealand]] forces under SCAP were organized into a sub-command known as [[:en:British Commonwealth Occupation Force|British Commonwealth Occupation Force]].
These actions led MacArthur to be viewed as the new Imperial force in Japan by many Japanese political and civilian figures, even being considered to be the rebirth of the ''[[shōgun]]''-style government<ref name="dower">{{cite book |author-link=John W. Dower|last=Dower |first=John W. |date=1999 |title=[[:en:Embracing Defeat|Embracing Defeat: Japan in the Wake of World War II]] |location=New York |publisher=[[:en:W. W. Norton|W. W. Norton]] |isbn=978-0-393-04686-1 |oclc=39143090}}</ref>{{rp|341}} which Japan was ruled under until the start of the [[Meiji Restoration]]. American biographer William Manchester argues that without MacArthur's leadership, Japan would not have been able to make the move from an imperial, totalitarian state, to a democracy. At his appointment, MacArthur announced that he sought to "restore security, dignity and self-respect" to the Japanese people.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Manchester|first1=William|title=American Caesar|date=1978|publisher=Little, Brown and Company|isbn=0-316-54498-1|url=https://archive.org/details/americancaesardo00manc |url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/americancaesardo00manc/page/n503 472]}}</ref>
MacArthur was also in charge of [[:en:United States Army Military Government in Korea|southern Korea]] from 1945 to 1948 due to the lack of clear orders or initiative from Washington, D.C. There was no plan or guideline given to MacArthur from the Joint Chiefs of Staff or the State Department on how to rule Korea, resulting in a tumultuous [[:en:Operation Blacklist Forty|3 year military occupation]] that led to the creation of the U.S.-friendly [[:en:Republic of Korea|Republic of Korea]] in 1948. He ordered Lieutenant General [[:en:John R. Hodge|John R. Hodge]], who accepted the surrender of Japanese forces in southern Korea in September 1945, to govern that area on SCAP's behalf and report to him in Tokyo.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.army.mil/books/wwii/MacArthur%20Reports/MacArthur%20V1%20Sup/ch3.htm |title=CHAPTER III: THE COMMAND STRUCTURE: AFPAC, FEC AND SCAP |website=history.army.mil |access-date=26 March 2021}}{{title missing|date=May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.army.mil/books/pd-c-02.htm |title=CHAPTER II:The House Divided |website=history.army.mil |access-date=26 March 2021}}</ref>
== General MacArthur == {{main |Douglas MacArthur}} [[File:MacArthur_arrives_at_Atsugi;ac01732.jpg|thumb|MacArthur arrives at Atsugi airfield, August 30th, 1945.]] SCAP is oftentimes synonymous with its appointed post war leader, American General Douglas MacArthur. MacArthur ruled Japan with a fairly lenient approach.
As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, MacArthur decided not to prosecute [[:en:Shiro Ishii|Shiro Ishii]] and all members of the [[:en:Unit 731|bacteriological research units]] in exchange for [[:en:germ warfare|germ warfare]] data based on [[:en:human experimentation|human experimentation]]. On May 6, 1947, he wrote to Washington that "additional data, possibly some statements from Ishii probably can be obtained by informing Japanese involved that information will be retained in intelligence channels and will not be employed as 'War Crimes' evidence."<ref>Gold, Hal (2004). ''Unit 731 testimony''. Boston: Tuttle. p. 109. {{ISBN|978-4-900737-39-6}}. {{OCLC|422879915}}.</ref> The deal was concluded in 1948.<ref>Drayton, Richard (May 10, 2005). "An Ethical Blank Cheque: British and US mythology about the second world war ignores our own crimes and legitimises Anglo-American war making". ''[[:en:The Guardian|The Guardian]]''. Archived from the original on January 11, 2012.</ref>
According to historian [[:en:Herbert Bix|Herbert Bix]] in ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]'', "MacArthur's truly extraordinary measures to save the Emperor from trial as a war criminal had a lasting and profoundly distorting impact on Japanese understanding of the lost war."<ref name=":0">[[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix, Herbert P.]] (2000). ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]''. New York: [[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]]. p. 562</ref> MacArthur's reasoning was that if the emperor were executed or sentenced to life imprisonment there would be a violent backlash and revolution from the Japanese of all social classes, and this would interfere with his primary goal of changing Japan from a militarist, feudal society to a pro-Western modern democracy. In a cable sent to General Dwight Eisenhower in February 1946, MacArthur stated that executing or imprisoning the emperor would require the use of one million occupation soldiers to keep the peace.<ref>How the Emperor Became Human (And MacArthur Became Divine)". ''longreads.com''. 11 November 2015. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref>
=== SCAP's relationship with Japanese leadership === [[File:Emperor Hirohito and General MacArthur.jpg|thumb|General MacArthur and Emperor Hirohito, 29th of September, 1945]] The relationship between Japanese leadership and SCAP was tense, as SCAP domineered the former on the path to post war reconstruction. MacArthur was focused on the task at hand, shown by his refusal to address the Japanese leadership or public directly, instead electing to go straight to and from his office every day, without stops. <ref>Watanabe Kenichi Olivier Mille Christine Watanabe ARTE France Kami Productions (Firm) Artline Films and Arte éditions (Firm) dirs. 2009. ''Japan the Emperor and the Army''. Icarus Films.</ref>
MacArthur and SCAP were adamant that the Emperor especially be shielded from responsibility for the war. MacArthur allowed the Emperor to issue statements that allowed for post war SCAP policy to be reframed as continued [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji restoration]], allowing the Emperor to cling to legitimacy. These views would be reflected in the first eight articles of the [[:en:Constitution of Japan|Constitution of Japan]].<ref name=":02">[[:en:Herbert Bix|Bix, Herbert P.]] (2000). ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]''. New York: [[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]]. p. 562</ref>
==Transforming Japan== A major [[:en:Land reform|Land reform]] was conducted, led by [[:en:Wolf Ladejinsky|Wolf Ladejinsky]] of MacArthur's SCAP staff; however, Ladejinsky himself stated that the true architect of the land reform was {{ill|Hiroo Wada|ja|3=和田博雄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hiroo Wada|qq=}}, then-[[:en:Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (Japan)|Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries]] from the [[:en:Japan Socialist Party|Japan Socialist Party]].<ref>{{citation |surname=Ness |given=Gayl D. |year=1967 |title=Review of the book ''Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy: Lord and Peasant in the Making of the Modern World'' |journal=American Sociological Review |volume=32 |issue=5 |pages=818–820 |doi=10.2307/2092029 |jstor=2092029 }}.</ref> Between 1947 and 1949, approximately {{convert|4700000|acre|sigfig=3|abbr=on}}, or 38% of Japan's cultivated land, was purchased from the landlords under the government's reform program, and {{convert|4600000|acre|sigfig=3|abbr=on}} was resold to the farmers who worked them. By 1950, 89% of all agricultural land was owner-operated and only 11% was tenant-operated.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=183–192}} MacArthur's efforts to encourage trade union membership met with phenomenal success, and by 1947, 48% of the non-agricultural workforce was unionized. Some of MacArthur's reforms were rescinded in 1948 when his unilateral control of Japan was ended by the increased involvement of the State Department.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=174–183}} During the Occupation, SCAP successfully, if not entirely, abolished many of the financial coalitions known as the [[:en:Zaibatsu|Zaibatsu]], which had previously monopolized industry.{{sfn|Schaller|1985|p=25}} Eventually, looser industrial groupings known as ''[[:en:Keiretsu|Keiretsu]]'' evolved. The reforms alarmed many in the U.S. Departments of Defense and State, who believed they conflicted with the prospect of Japan and its industrial capacity as a bulwark against the spread of communism in Asia.{{sfn|James|1985|pp=222–224, 252–254}}
Japan's hereditary peerage, called [[kazoku]], that lasted for over a millennium in different but essentially similar forms, was abolished by the new Japanese constitution that was heavily influenced by MacArthur. This was similar to the European peerage system involving princes, barons and counts that were not part of the royal family. Also, the extended royal family, called [[:en:Ōke|Ōke]] and [[:en:Shinnōke|Shinnōke]], was abolished and stripped of all rights and privileges, transforming into commoners immediately. The only Japanese that were allowed to call themselves a part of royalty or nobility after the U.S. occupation were the emperor and about 20 of his [[Imperial House of Japan#List of current members|direct family members]]. This action by MacArthur and the writers of the constitution helped transform Japan drastically by abolishing all of the old extended royal family class and the nobility class.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/macarthur-occupation-japan-and-constitution/ |title=Occupation of Japan and the New Constitution | American Experience | PBS |website=www.pbs.org |access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>
==Welfare programs== One of the largest of the SCAP programs was Public Health and Welfare, headed by US Army Colonel Crawford F. Sams. Working with the SCAP staff of 150, Sams directed the welfare work of the American doctors, and organized entirely new Japanese medical welfare systems along American lines. The Japanese population was in a poor state: most people were badly worn down, doctors and medicines were very scarce, and sanitary systems had been bombed out in larger cities. Sams' earliest priorities were in distributing food supplies from the United States. Millions of refugees from the defunct overseas empire were pouring in, often in bad physical shape, with a high risk of introducing [[:en:Smallpox|Smallpox]], [[typhus]] and [[:en:Cholera|Cholera]]. The outbreaks that did occur were localized, as emergency immunization, quarantine, sanitation, and delousing prevented massive epidemics. Sams, who was promoted to Brigadier General in 1948, worked with Japanese officials to establish vaccine laboratories, reorganize hospitals along American lines, upgrade medical and nursing schools, and bring together Japanese, international, and US teams that dealt with disasters, child care, and health insurance. He set up an Institute of Public Health for educating public health workers and a National Institute of Health for research, and set up statistical divisions and data collection systems.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Crawford F. |last=Sams |title="Medic": The Mission of an American Military Doctor in Occupied Japan and Wartorn Korea |date=1998 |isbn=978-1-315-50371-4 |publisher=Routledge}}</ref>
== Constitution == {{Main |Constitution of Japan}}
One of the most significant actions of SCAP during the occupation was the drafting of a new Japanese constitution. One of MacArthur's top priorities was an overhaul of the existing [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]], to bring the country in line with its new democratic government. He gave the task of drafting the constitution to his officers, frustrated by the slowness of legislators. They would finish the task within a week, and presenting the new constitution as a wholesale amendment to the [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]]. It provided protections to the Emperor, placing him at the head of the state. It was ratified November of 1946 and went into effect May 3rd, 1947. It remains the oldest unamended constitution in the world. <ref>"The Anomalous Life of the Japanese Constitution". ''Nippon.com''. 15 August 2017. Archived from the original on 11 August 2019.</ref>
=== Article 9 === The most polarizing aspect of the Japanese constitution, a part that still sees debate to this day, is the presence of [[:en:Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution|Article 9]], a clause covering the status of the Japanese military. The clause outlaws belligerency and prohibits the establishment of organized armed forces by the government. Despite this, Japan maintains a "[[:en:Japan Self-Defense Forces|self defense force]]" (a de facto defensive military) of around 250,000 active personnel. Article 9 and the [[:en:Japan Self-Defense Forces|JSDF]] are both hotly contested subjects of debates in modern Japanese politics, as pacifists see the JSDF and [[:en:Military history of Japan|military involvement]] in foreign countries as unconstitutional, while nationalists seek [[:en:Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution|Article 9]]'s removal and a wider rearmament of Japan.
==War crimes issues== SCAP arrested 28 suspected war criminals on account of crimes against peace, but it did not conduct the Tokyo Trials; the [[:en:International Military Tribunal for the Far East|International Military Tribunal for the Far East]] was responsible instead.<ref>{{cite book |first=Timothy P. |last=Maga |title=Judgment at Tokyo: The Japanese War Crimes Trials |date=2001 |publisher=University Press of Kentucky |isbn=978-0-8131-2177-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first=Yuki |last=Tanaka |display-authors=etal |title=Beyond Victor's Justice? The Tokyo War Crimes Trial Revisited|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nOIzDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA149|year=2011|publisher=BRILL|pages=149–50 |isbn=978-90-04-21591-7}}</ref> [[:en:President of the United States|President]] [[:en:Harry S. Truman|Harry Truman]] had negotiated Japanese surrender on the condition the Emperor would not be executed or put on trial. SCAP carried out that policy.<ref>{{cite book|first=Paul |last=Ham|title=Hiroshima Nagasaki: The Real Story of the Atomic Bombings and Their Aftermath|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5FZGAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA79|year=2014|publisher=St. Martin's Press|pages=79–80 |isbn=978-1-4668-4747-7}}</ref>
As soon as November 26, 1945, MacArthur confirmed to Admiral [[:en:Mitsumasa Yonai|Mitsumasa Yonai]] that the emperor's abdication would not be necessary.{{r|dower|page1=323}} Before the war crimes trials actually convened, SCAP, the IPS and officials from [[:en:Hirohito|Hirohito]]'s [[Shōwa period|Shōwa]] government worked behind the scenes not only to prevent the imperial family being indicted, but also to slant the testimony of the defendants to ensure that no one implicated the Emperor. High officials in court circles and the Shōwa government collaborated with Allied GHQ in compiling lists of prospective [[:en:war criminals|war criminals]], while the individuals arrested as ''Class A'' suspects and incarcerated in [[:en:Sugamo Prison|Sugamo Prison]] solemnly vowed to protect their sovereign against any possible taint of war responsibility.{{r|dower|page1=325}}
As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, MacArthur also decided not to prosecute [[:en:Shiro Ishii|Shiro Ishii]] and all members of the [[:en:Unit 731|bacteriological research units]] in exchange for [[:en:germ warfare|germ warfare]] data based on [[:en:human experimentation|human experimentation]]. On May 6, 1947, he wrote to Washington that "additional data, possibly some statements from Ishii probably can be obtained by informing Japanese involved that information will be retained in intelligence channels and will not be employed as "War Crimes" evidence."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gold |first1=Hal |title=Unit 731 testimony |date=2004 |publisher=Tuttle |location=Boston |isbn=978-4-900737-39-6 |oclc=422879915 |page=[https://archive.org/details/unit731testimony00halg/page/109 109] |url=https://archive.org/details/unit731testimony00halg/page/109 }}</ref> The deal was concluded in 1948.<ref>{{cite news |last=Drayton |first=Richard |date=May 10, 2005 |url=http://www.commondreams.org/views05/0510-24.htm |title=An Ethical Blank Cheque: British and US mythology about the second world war ignores our own crimes and legitimises Anglo-American war making |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111112521/http://www.commondreams.org/views05/0510-24.htm |archive-date=January 11, 2012 |work=[[:en:The Guardian|The Guardian]]}}</ref>
According to historian [[:en:Herbert Bix|Herbert Bix]] in ''[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]]'', "MacArthur's truly extraordinary measures to save the Emperor from trial as a war criminal had a lasting and profoundly distorting impact on Japanese understanding of the lost war."<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Herbert Bix |last=Bix |first=Herbert P. |date=2000 |title=[[:en:Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan|Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan]] |location=New York |publisher=[[:en:HarperCollins|HarperCollins]] |isbn=978-0-06-019314-0 |oclc=247018161 |page=545}}</ref> MacArthur's reasoning was if the emperor were executed or sentenced to life imprisonment there would be a violent backlash and revolution from the Japanese from all social classes and this would interfere with his primary goal to change Japan from a militarist, feudal society to a pro-Western modern democracy. In a cable sent to General Dwight Eisenhower in February 1946 MacArthur said executing or imprisoning the emperor would require the use of one million occupation soldiers to keep the peace.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://longreads.com/2015/11/11/how-the-emperor-became-human-and-macarthur-became-divine/ |title=How the Emperor Became Human (And MacArthur Became Divine) |website=longreads.com |date= 11 November 2015|access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref>
==Media censorship== Above the political and economic control SCAP had for the seven years following Japan's surrender, SCAP also had strict control over all of the Japanese media, under the formation of the [[:en:Civil Censorship Detachment|Civil Censorship Detachment]] (CCD) of SCAP. The CCD eventually banned a total of 31 topics from all forms of media.{{r|dower|page1=341}} These topics included:
* Criticism of SCAP (individuals and the organization). * All Allied countries. * Criticism of Allied policy pre- and post-war. * Any form of [[:en:Empire of Japan|imperial]] propaganda. * Defense of [[:en:Japanese war crimes|war criminals]]. * Praise of "undemocratic" [[:en:Form of government|forms of government]], though praise of SCAP itself was permitted. * The [[:en:Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]]. * [[:en:Underground economy|Black market]] activities. * Open discussion of allied diplomatic relations ([[Soviet Union–United States relations]]).
Although some of the CCD censorship laws considerably relaxed towards the end of SCAP, some topics, like the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, were taboo until 1952 at the end of the occupation.
== Approach to the Japanese Communist Party and Post-War Reforms ==
{{Essay-like|section|date=July 2023}}
MacArthur legalized the [[:en:Japanese Communist Party|Japanese Communist Party]] despite reservations from the United States government and invited them to take part in the [[:en:1946 Japanese general election|1946 election]], which was also the first ever Japanese election to allow women to vote. He ordered the release of all political prisoners of the Imperial Japanese era, including communist prisoners. MacArthur approved the first May Day parade in 11 years in 1946. On the day before the May Day celebrations, which would involve 300,000 Japanese communists demonstrating with red flags and pro-Marxism chants in front of the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]] and the [[:en:DN Tower 21|Dai-Ichi Building]], a group of would-be assassins led by Hideo Tokayama that planned to assassinate MacArthur with hand grenades and pistols on May Day was stopped and some of its members arrested. Despite this plot the May Day demonstrations went on. MacArthur stopped the Communist Party from gaining any popularity in Japan by releasing their members from prison, conducting landmark land reform for the rural Japanese farmers and peasants, and allowing the communists to freely participate in elections. In the 1946 election they won only 6 seats.<ref>Morris Jr., Seymour. ''Supreme Commander: MacArthur's Triumph in Japan''. Page 169-173</ref><ref>"MacArthur Plot Alarms Japanese; They See Possible Repercussions; JAPANESE FEARFUL ON M'ARTHUR PLOT Timed for Demonstration Plotters Still at Large". ''The New York Times''. May 1946. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref><ref>"Gettysburg Times - Google News Archive Search". ''news.google.com''. Retrieved 18 April 2021.</ref>
== Legacy ==
[[File:Yoshida_signs_San_Francisco_Peace_Treaty.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Shigeru Yoshida|Shigeru Yoshida]], [[:en:Prime Minister of Japan|Prime Minister of Japan]] signing the San Francisco Peace Treaty on September 8, 1951]] MacArthur handed over power to the Japanese government in 1949, but remained in Japan until relieved by President [[:en:Harry S. Truman|Harry S. Truman]] on 11 April 1951, after which he was succeeded as SCAP by General [[:en:Matthew Ridgway|Matthew Ridgway]]. The [[:en:San Francisco Peace Treaty|San Francisco Peace Treaty]], signed on 8 September 1951, marked the end of the Allied occupation, and when it went into effect on 28 April 1952, Japan was once again an independent state. The position of SCAP was effectively abolished on 1 July 1957 with the disbandment of the [[:en:Far East Command (United States)|Far East Command]]. However, the United States continued to administer some Japanese islands after that with, for example, Okinawa being continually under US administration until 1972.<ref>USFJ (May 13, 2022). "United States Forces Japan". US Forces Japan. Retrieved 2019-02-20.</ref>
=== Active US military presence === {{Main |United States Forces Japan}} All branches of the United States military forces are still present in Japan today. They primarily function in a support role, providing defense for Japan and the surrounding region, per the agreements of the [[Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan|US-Japan Mutual Security Treaty.]] The [[:en:United States Forces Japan|United States Forces Japan]] consists of around 50,000 service members deployed all over Japan to protect Japanese and US interests alike. This has led to tension at times between Japanese citizens and American servicemen, with incidents frequently occurring between locals and servicemen and crimes frequently committed by servicemen against locals, such as the [[:en:1995 Okinawa rape incident|1995 Okinawa rape incident]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spitzer |first=Kirk |title=Tens of thousands protest on Okinawa to close key U.S. bases in Japan |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2016/06/19/okinawa-protest-marines/86110434/ |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2024-06-28 |title=Second U.S. service member in months charged with rape in Japan's Okinawa: "We are outraged" - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/second-us-soldier-japan-charged-sexual-assault-okinawa/ |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref> These incidents led to plans to relocate military bases in [[:en:Okinawa Prefecture|Okinawa]], namely [[:en:Marine Corps Air Station Futenma|Marine Corps Air Station Futenma]], as three quarters of all USFJ installations are located in the prefecture, despite its small size. However, the plan has been delayed due to protests at the site designated for its relocation on another part of the island.<ref name=":1" />
